newsitem.title: HUNGARY: EXPORT OUTLOOKS DEPRESS HUNGARY BCE GRAINS FUTURES.
newsitem.headline: EXPORT OUTLOOKS DEPRESS HUNGARY BCE GRAINS FUTURES.

text.p: Most grain futures continued to fall on the Budapest Commodity Exchange and were far from bottoming out as the selling side continued to dominate, traders said on Wednesday.
"Pessimistic export outlooks also mean that present stocks have to be financed and stored, generating additional expenses, so it could still be better to sell," said Gabor Herczeg of LaSalle.
Milling wheat prices dropped by 350 to 400 forints to end at 26,740 forints for January 1997 and 23,400 for December 1997.

"There are some 0.5 million tonnes of wheat stuck in the country," said Herczeg, adding that prices for the 1996 crop would probably bottom out somewhere in the $120 to $130 bracket (19,500 to 21,200 forints at current exchange rates).
Maize prices also dropped by limit for all maturities and outlooks were even more pessimistic there, traders said.
"Maize prices could even go below production costs," Herczeg said.
He added that according to a November IGC report planted areas are up in Yugoslavia, Bulgaria, Ukraine and Hungary and this would change the status of the region.
"It will become a region to offer, rather than take up (maize)," he said.
Maize futures prices ended at 18,900 forints for March 1997 and 21,000 forints for December 1997 but were still overpriced compared with international markets.
Total grains turnover was 709 million forints or 1,599 lots, of which 891 lots were milling wheat and 578 maize.
(Lot size is 20,000 kgs for all contracts. $=162.86 forints)
